notes.short: The believers pictured as a letter from Christ
notes.about: Paul asks if he needs letters of recommendation, as some people do. The believers at Corinth are his letter, a letter from Christ, written with the Spirit instead of ink, on human hearts instead of tablets of stone. He carries the picture through: Christ is the writer, and Paul wrote it out.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: you are a letter from Christ
figure.means: the believers at Corinth, whose faith is Christ’s own work through Paul’s preaching, and so the proof that Christ sent him

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verses under Allegory. Calvin says Paul pursues the metaphor, making Christ the author and himself the instrument. Barnes says Paul continues and varies the image. Clarke sets out the parts of the figure: Christ dictates, the apostle writes, hearts take the writing, the Spirit makes the marks. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott): the metaphor shifts, and Christ is the real writer.

cites.at: Allegory, or Continued Metaphor and Hypocatastasis, p. 750
cites.quote: For other examples, see Joh 4:35 ... 2Co 3:2-3 ; 2Co 5:1 , etc.; 10:3-5; 11:2.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Pursuing the metaphor, he says that the Epistle of which he speaks was written by Christ, inasmuch as the faith of the Corinthians was his work. He says that it was ministered by him, as if meaning by this, that he had been in the place of ink and pen. In fine, he makes Christ the author and himself the instrument
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: That which Christ has sent to be our testimonial. He has given this letter of recommendation. ... Christ, in writing this epistle, so to speak, has used our aid; or employed us as amanuenses (copyists). Written not with ink - Paul continues and varies the image in regard to this "epistle," so that he may make the testimony borne to his fidelity and success more striking and emphatic.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Ye are the writing, but Christ used me as the pen; Christ dictated, and I wrote ... See the parts of this figurative speech: 1. Jesus Christ dictates. 2. The apostle writes. 3. The hearts of the Corinthians are the substance on which the writing is made. And, 4. The Holy Spirit produces that influence by which the traces are made, and the mark becomes evident.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The metaphor appears to shift its ground from the subjective to the objective. It is not only as written in his heart, but as seen and known by others, that they (the Corinthians) are as a letter of commendation. They are as a letter which Christ had written as with the finger of God. ... He had been, that is, as the amanuensis of that letter, but Christ was the real writer.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Moses’ veil, carried from his face to the heart
notes.about: Paul takes the veil Moses put over his face and carries it through the passage. The same veil remains when the old covenant is read; it lies over the heart, and is taken away whenever anyone turns to the Lord. Believers, with unveiled faces, reflect the Lord’s glory and are changed into His image.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant
figure.means: the dullness that keeps hearers of the old covenant from seeing its true end, a veil taken away only in Christ

notes.evidence: E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott) says the figure changes as it goes: the veil is no longer on the lawgiver’s face but on the hearers’ hearts, hiding the Law’s true meaning. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says Paul passes from the fact to the truth it symbolized. Barnes says a veil lies over the Old Testament as over Moses’ face; Calvin, that the veil was an emblem of the people’s dullness.
notes.limit: The note does not claim that Moses himself meant the veil as a sign; Paul draws the lesson from the history.

cites.quote: The figure is passing through a kind of dissolving change. There is still a veil between the hearers of the Law and its true meaning; but the veil is no longer on the face of the law-giver, but on their hearts ... It is, the Apostle says, because the veil of prejudice and tradition hinders them from seeing the truth that the Jews of his own time still think of the Law as permanent
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: Paul here ( Co2 3:13 ) passes from the literal fact to the truth symbolized by it, the blindness of Jews and Judaizers to the ultimate end of the law: stating that Moses put on the veil that they might not look steadfastly at (Christ, Rom 10:4 ) the end of that (law) which (like Moses' glory) is done away. Not that Moses had this purpose
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A veil seems to be thrown over the Old Testament when they read it, as there was over the face of Moses ... In the manifestation, or appearance of Jesus the Messiah, the veil is removed. ... and as the face of Moses could have been distinctly seen if the veil on his face had been removed, so it is in regard to the true meaning of the Old Testament by the coming of the Messiah.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: By this he means, that that dulness of vision was not for a single hour merely, but prefigured what the condition of the nation would be in time to come. “That veil with which Moses covered his face, when publishing the law, was the emblem of a stupidity, that would come upon that people ... God has shown long ago under the type of the veil, that it would be so.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.about: The second line answers the first with its opposite. Whoever sows little reaps a small harvest, and whoever sows generously reaps a generous one. Paul applies the farmer's rule to giving.

lines.words: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly,
and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.

original.note: In Paul's Greek, the word for “generously” is “blessings” (eulogiais), set against the word for “sparingly”.

notes.evidence: Calvin reads the verse as a comparison of giving with sowing and sets the two lines side by side: whoever sows sparingly gets a poor harvest, and whoever sows bountifully a bountiful one. He adds that Paul here sets blessing against sparing.

cites.quote: He now commends alms-giving by a beautiful similitude, comparing it to sowing. ... He that sows sparingly will have a poor harvest, corresponding to the sowing: he that sows bountifully and with a full hand, will reap a correspondingly bountiful harvest. ... He again contrasts here blessing with sparing, as he had previously done with niggardliness.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “Forgive me this wrong!”: said in irony
notes.about: Paul asks how the Corinthians fell short of other churches, and names only one thing: he was never a burden to them. Asking pardon for that “wrong” is irony, since he had spared them the cost of supporting him. It can also be read as a rebuke of how they had treated him.

figure.name: Irony
figure.means: that sparing them the cost of supporting him was no true wrong done to them

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the words under irony spoken by men. Barnes calls the verse a striking mixture of sarcasm and irony: in one thing only were they behind other churches, in not having been burdened with the privilege of supporting Paul. Calvin says the exception is put by way of irony, since serving them without pay was one more kindness, and he sees in it a rebuke of their ingratitude.
notes.limit: Not every writer hears only irony here: some take the words as a real apology, or partly one, for not letting them support him.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Human Irony, p. 814
cites.quote: “Forgive me this wrong.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This verse contains a striking mixture of sarcasm and irony ... In one respect only are you inferior - it is in this, that you have not been burdened with the privilege of supporting me.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Here is an aggravation of their ingratitude ... He subjoins one exception — that he had not been burdensome to them; and this, by way of irony, for in reality this was over and above so many acts of kindness, which he had conferred upon them — that he had served them gratuitously. ... he sharply reproves pride so frantic. Forgive me this wrong, says he. For they were doubly ungrateful
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Weak and strong at once, by Christ's power
notes.about: Paul delights in weaknesses and says “when I am weak, then I am strong.” The words seem to clash, yet they hold: pressed by trials and weak in himself, he is made strong by the Lord, whose power rests on him (verse 9).

figure.name: Oxymoron
figure.words: when I am weak, then I am strong
figure.means: when Paul is weak in himself and pressed by trials, the Lord's power makes him strong

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the words under Oxymoron: folly to the natural man, yet true to those who know it. Plumptre (Ellicott) calls them another paradox like those of 6:9-10: the greatest weakness may even be the condition of strength. Barnes grants that joy in affliction can seem a paradox; he, Calvin and Clarke read the weakness as trial and lack in Paul himself and the strength as what God supplies.

cites.quote: “When I am weak, then am I strong.” This is folly to the natural man, but blessed truth to those who know by experience the true wisdom.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: He had learnt to add another paradox to those of 2Co 6:9-10 , and to feel that the greatest weakness was not only compatible with the highest strength, but might be the very condition of its energy.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: There is often real pleasure in affliction, paradoxical as it may appear. ... When I feel weak; when I am subjected to trial, and nature faints and fails, then strength is imparted to me, and I am enabled to bear all.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The more deficiency there is in me, so much the more liberally does the Lord, from his strength, supply me with whatever he sees to be needful for me. ... be weak in himself that he may be strong in the Lord.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: For when I am weak - most oppressed with trials and afflictions, then am I strong; God supporting my mind with his most powerful influences, causing me to rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Light, brief trouble set against weighty glory
notes.about: Paul sets each part of present trouble against its answer in the glory to come: light against weight, a moment against eternity, affliction against glory. Set side by side, the trouble looks small beside the glory it is producing.

figure.name: Antithesis
figure.words: light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory
figure.means: present trouble, light and brief, set against the glory to come, weighty and eternal

original.note: In Paul's Greek “light” stands as a noun, the lightness of our affliction, and so answers the weight of glory more closely.

notes.evidence: E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) reads the present lightness of our affliction, which he says better keeps the balanced antithesis of the clauses. Barnes says Paul set the trials of this life and the glories of heaven in emphatic contrast. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) sets the lightness against the weight; Calvin says Paul compares present miseries with future felicity.

cites.quote: More accurately, the present lightness of our affliction. This is at once more literally in accord with the Greek, and better sustains the balanced antithesis of the clauses.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: His object is to contrast this with the glory that awaited him, as being heavy, and as being also eternal. … Paul has set in most beautiful and emphatic contrast the trials of this life and the glories of heaven.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: "The lightness of affliction" (he does not express "burden" after "light"; the Greek is "the light of affliction") contrasts beautifully with the "weight of the glory."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Paul, with the view of shaking us off from a carnal attachment to the present life, draws a comparison between present miseries and future felicity. … For this comparison makes that light which previously seemed heavy, and makes that brief and momentary which seemed of boundless duration.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The body as a tent, and a house from God
notes.about: Paul pictures the body as a tent that will be taken down, and sets against it a building from God, an eternal house in heaven. Then the picture turns to clothing: in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed, not unclothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: the earthly tent we live in is dismantled
figure.means: the death of the mortal body, a frail dwelling lived in for a short time and then taken down

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists 2 Corinthians 5:1 onward under Allegory. Calvin calls the tent a metaphor for the body, a frail hut for a few days. Barnes says Paul changes the metaphor from a dwelling to a garment. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says Paul the tentmaker takes the image from his trade. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott) says the tent shows how brief the dwelling is.
notes.limit: The writers differ on what the house from God is: the raised body, or the soul’s blessed state after death, completed at the resurrection. The note does not decide between them.

cites.at: Allegory, or Continued Metaphor and Hypocatastasis, p. 750
cites.quote: For other examples, see Joh 4:35 ... 2Co 5:1 , etc.; 10:3-5; 11:2.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: For as tabernacles are constructed, for a temporary purpose, of slight materials ... so the mortal body is given to men as a frail hut, to be inhabited by them for a few days. The same metaphor is made use of, also, by Peter ... the blessed condition of the soul after death is the commencement of this building, and the glory of the final resurrection is the consummation of it.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: There is evidently here a change of the metaphor which gives an apparent harshness to the construction. One idea of the apostle is, that the body here, and the spiritual body hereafter, is a house or a dwelling. Here he speaks of it as a garment which may be put on or laid off and of himself as earnestly desiring to put on the immortal clothing or vestment which was in heaven.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: "House" expresses more permanency than belongs to the body; therefore the qualification, "of the tabernacle" (implying that it is shifting, not stationary), is added ... Paul, as a tent-maker, uses an image taken from his trade ( Act 18:3 ). ... A solid building, not a temporary tabernacle or tent.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Better, be broken up, as more in harmony with the image of the tent. ... A new train of imagery begins to rise in his mind ... The modification introduced by the idea of the “tent” emphasises the transitory character of the habitation. “What if the tent be broken up?” He, the true inward man, who dwells in the tent will find a more permanent, an eternal, home in heaven

notes.short: A common saying: sow sparingly, reap sparingly
notes.about: Urging the Corinthians to give, Paul sets before them a saying from the farm: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. Giving is like sowing. What is given may seem lost, like seed in the ground, but in time it brings a harvest in proportion to it. Verse 10 speaks again of seed and harvest.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly
figure.means: giving to those in need: what is given seems lost, like seed in the ground, but it is returned in proportion to what was given

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verses among proverbs which appear for the first time in Scripture and have since passed into general use. Barnes says the words have all the appearance of a proverb, and that it is in giving as in farming: money given is like seed committed to the earth, and returns with increase. Clarke calls it a plain maxim, with almsgiving pictured as seed sown that bears a crop.
notes.limit: Paul does not quote the words as a known saying. One of the writers judges they were already a proverb; another lists them among proverbs that first appear in Scripture.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 765
cites.quote: See other examples of such Proverbs in Pro 11:27 ... 1Co 10:12 ; 1Co 15:33 . 2Co 9:6-7 . 2Th 3:10 . Tit 1:15
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This expression has all the appearance of a proverb, and doubtless is such. ... Paul here says that it is in giving as it is in agriculture. A man that sows little must expect to reap little. ... So it is in giving. Money given in alms ... is money bestowed in a way similar to the act of committing seed to the earth. It will be returned again in some way with an abundant increase.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This is a plain maxim: no man can expect to reap but in proportion as he has sowed. And here almsgiving is represented as a seed sown, which shall bring forth a crop. If the sowing be liberal, and the seed good, the crop shall be so too.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Seed and bread, then seed and harvest
notes.about: Four lines take turns. The first answers the third: He who supplies seed to the sower will supply and multiply your store of seed. The second answers the fourth: bread for food, then the harvest of your righteousness.

lines.words: Now He who supplies seed to the sower
will supply and multiply your store of seed
and will increase the harvest of your righteousness.

notes.evidence: Jebb sets the verse out as an alternate quatrain and traces a rising order in its terms: a term is advanced upon in the parallel line by two verbs, and a term of the second line is answered in the fourth.

cites.quote: The beauty of that alternate quatrain it is scarcely necessary to indicate to any attentive reader. There is a fine ascending gradation in the terms of it: … in the parallel line, it is advanced upon by the two verbs … of the second line, we have, in the fourth line
cites.read: the 1820 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/sacredliterature00jebb

notes.short: Paul’s work pictured as a war on strongholds
notes.about: Paul pictures his work as a war. Though he lives in the flesh, he does not fight by the flesh; his weapons have divine power to tear down strongholds. Arguments raised against the knowledge of God are torn down, and every thought is taken captive, as prisoners are taken in war, to obey Christ.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world
figure.means: the spiritual means God gives His servants, such as true teaching made mighty by His Spirit, set against all that is raised up against Him

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verses under Allegory. Calvin says Paul compares the ministry of the gospel to a warfare, a most apt similitude, with spiritual weapons. Clarke says Paul often uses the metaphor of a warfare for a minister’s life. Barnes says the figure is taken from military conquest. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott) says the soldier’s word grows into an elaborate figure.

cites.at: Allegory, or Continued Metaphor and Hypocatastasis, p. 750
cites.quote: For other examples, see Joh 4:35 ... 2Co 5:1 , etc.; 10:3-5; 11:2.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The warfare, accordingly, is spiritual. ... In comparing the ministry of the gospel to a warfare, he uses a most apt similitude. ... At the same time, if you would have a full enumeration of spiritual weapons, doctrine must be conjoined with zeal, and a good conscience with the efficacy of the Spirit, and with other necessary graces.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The apostle often uses the metaphor of a warfare to represent the life and trials of a Christian minister. ...
